prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep my configuration unchanged: a single-part prize for GLP-1 physiology to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific chain is unbroken and unusually well confirmed: proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, its insulinotropic and appetite-related actions in humans, receptor biology, and then durable receptor agonism with independently replicated glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. Recognition after decades of evidence is mature and arguably overdue. All six of us converged on this configuration from independent opening ballots, and I weigh that only as a prompt to test the case harder, not as merit. The test I applied is the one the chair set: does the case survive if the credit is narrowed to what the supplied record can support? It does. Holst (human physiology of secretion and action), Drucker (receptor and proglucagon-derived peptide biology) and Mojsov (the active peptide) cover the discovery arc, and a citation worded around the physiology and the active form, with the therapies named as what it made possible, honours the drugs without crediting the drug-design step as a laureate contribution. Nothing in round 1 gave me a reason to move to a two-part prize, because any second achievement would force a cut inside the GLP-1 trio.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and I have not resolved it. The Mojsov versus Habener priority question for the active peptide cannot be settled from the supplied record, and all six of us are leaning on recollection of the history. If I am wrong about Mojsov, the trio would have to change. Excluding Knudsen leaves the long-acting analogue design, which turned the biology into medicines, outside the credit, and a physiology-only prize can be criticised as celebrating the science while skipping the drug. Habener and other early peptide workers are outside the credited list. Long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications are still being characterised, so the citation should not overclaim.

responses.point: Moved from TNF blockade first to the GLP-1 trio, asks that the citation name the therapies that followed so that excluding Knudsen does not read as a verdict on the drugs, and says the Mojsov priority claim should not be called settled merely because we share recollections.
responses.response: I accept both points. I have adopted citation wording that states the discoveries as the physiology and active form of GLP-1 and then says they made incretin-based therapies possible, which answers your concern without moving a drug developer into a discovery slot. On Mojsov, I agree we have not verified the priority record and I will not claim it is settled. My position is conditional: if the committee concluded that the identification of the active peptide cannot be credited to Mojsov without Habener, the name list would need to be reopened, and I would then lean toward holding the prize until the attribution is clearer rather than defaulting to Knudsen. I also still place CAR-T ahead of TNF blockade as an alternative, but your point about Eshhar and unresolved toxicity is fair and is why CAR-T stays an alternative and not a second part.

responses.point: As chair, treats Holst, Drucker and Mojsov as the defensible academic core, lists Knudsen only as an alternative third slot, and flags that optogenetics omits at least three credible names and that the priority history rests on memory.
responses.response: I agree with your framing and with your caution about the record. Your question on Knudsen versus Mojsov is the right one, and my answer is Mojsov: the discovery-level identification of the active form is what the later biology and the drugs rest on, whereas the analogue design is an industrial programme that is harder to attribute to one person and would break the clean discovery logic of the award. On optogenetics I have not moved. I hold it as an alternative because no three-person subset of Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenböck and Nagel is defensible on principle, and I would not let that fairness problem attach to a second part of a prize that is otherwise uncontested.

responses.point: Prefers the clean single-achievement GLP-1 prize, sees no case yet for a second achievement that outweighs it, and notes that excluding Knudsen leaves out the engineering without which the discovery would not have become a therapy.
responses.response: I agree that a single-achievement prize is the cleaner option, and round 1 did not produce a second part that I could defend. I also agree with you that the pharmaceutical engineering is a real part of the story, but I read that as a reason for careful citation wording and not for adding a name. In round 1 I suggested CAR-T as the preferable second part if the committee wanted one, and I still think that is the best-supported choice, but the three-person cap means a second part would cost one of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov, and I do not think CAR-T justifies that cost this year.

responses.point: Keeps the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) as a fall-back if the GLP-1 credit cannot be defended, and would hold optogenetics as an alternative rather than combine it with GLP-1.
responses.response: I take your fall-back seriously, and I agree that Walter and Mori are a compact pair. My disagreement is about what triggers it. If the Mojsov question were unresolvable, the UPR would not be the natural replacement for me, because its disease relevance and therapeutic translation are still developing and the mammalian PERK and ATF6 branches are outside the credit. I would rank CAR-T ahead of it as the alternative with demonstrated clinical effect. I agree with you that optogenetics should not be folded into a combined prize with GLP-1. That would widen the attribution dispute without strengthening either part.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is defensible against the Habener group's claim; I rely on recollection and the supplied record does not settle it.
Whether a prize centred on physiology and peptide identification, with Knudsen outside the laureate list, will be read as under-crediting drug development despite the citation wording.
Whether CAR-T (June, Sadelain, Rosenberg) is fair given Eshhar's chimeric-receptor concept lies outside the credited names and Rosenberg's link to CAR-specific engineering is indirect.
Whether optogenetics could ever be resolved within three names given Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck would be excluded.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén, who are Karolinska Institutet colleagues, but none of that work concerns any shortlisted candidate or credited name, and shared institution or topic is not a recusal issue by itself. I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, June, Sadelain, Rosenberg or the optogenetics names. My single-cell and RNA-processing field is not close to any shortlisted ballot.
